decision_rule: PRIMARY (preregistered): 'QUBO helps' iff BOTH hold on the 16+16 runs: (a) mean scaffold fidelity (Spearman rank corr of pairwise centroid distances at compress-end vs best-known optimum, computed exactly as in when-hardening-helps A12) is higher for the QUBO-warm-started arm than the random-init arm, one-sided Mann-Whitney U p < 0.05; AND (b) mean final container L is lower for the QUBO arm, one-sided Mann-Whitney U p < 0.05. If either fails, report as NULL: classical QUBO scaffold sampling does not improve hardening outcomes at this grid resolution. SECONDARY (exploratory): fidelity distribution of the raw QUBO samples (pre-hardening) vs random inits, to separate 'better arrangement' from 'tighter start'.
hypothesis: Scaffolds sampled by optimizing a coordinate-based disk-packing QUBO (classical simulated annealing) are better warm starts for hardening than random disk initializations: they yield higher scaffold fidelity and lower final L on squ-in-squ n=11.

qubo.decode: argmax per run; occupied cells -> continuous positions (cell centers); rotations random (seeded)
qubo.note: CLASSICAL simulated annealing only (dimod). NEVER label this output as quantum.
qubo.sa_seeds: 1..16 (one independent SA run per harden seed)
qubo.variables: y[g] in {0,1} for each grid cell; E = P_card*(sum y - 11)^2 + P_over*sum_{overlapping pairs} y_g*y_h - c_tight*sum_g (1 - r_g^2/r_max^2) y_g

question: Does better scaffold sampling (via QUBO optimization, solved classically) improve hardening outcomes vs random scaffolds?

title: Classical QUBO scaffold sampling for hardening warm starts
